public_rationale: This is a conditional argument, not a dated forecast. To score it, we would need a named system shown to lack a robust model of chess rules. We would then need to test whether that same system learned 'all it needs to know' about time, finance and everyday life from data alone. Marcus names no system and defines neither 'robust' nor 'all it needs to know'. So we cannot show the antecedent held, and the consequent has no plain test. Under the rules for conditional forecasts, the outcome is not adjudicable.
limitations: The claim reads mostly as rhetoric about learning from data, not as a testable forecast.
Benchmarks on temporal reasoning exist, but none tie their results to chess-rule competence in the same system.

our_interpretation: Read as a conditional forecast: a system that fails to learn a robust model of chess rules from data will not learn, from statistical training alone, everything it needs about time, finance, shopping and the changing world.
The antecedent needs a named system shown to lack a robust chess-rules model; the post does not name one or define 'robust'.
The consequent 'all it needs to know' has no stated measure or threshold, so there is no ordinary test of whether a system has met it.
criteria.support_condition: A named system shown to lack a robust model of chess rules is also shown, by public evaluation, to fail reliable reasoning about time, finance and everyday world dynamics despite training only on big data.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A named system shown to lack a robust model of chess rules is shown, by public evaluation, to reason reliably about time, finance and everyday world dynamics after statistical training alone.
